title: The Last Great American Novel
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/ed-simon
text:
Eleven days before two Boeing 767s piloted by Al Qaeda terrorists slammed into the World Trade Center, killing 2,606 people, the publisher Farrar, Straus and Giroux, its offices less than two miles away, released Jonathan Franzen’s The Corrections, a 568-page doorstopper that was its author’s grand attempt at social realism. Twenty-five years on, the book, written in an America on the verge of being transformed, remains connected with the twisted iron and pulverized concrete of September 11, seemingly anticipated by its second sentence: “You could feel it: something terrible was going to happen.” 

A-J Aronstein, writing in 2012 in The Point, noted soberly that the hijacked planes rendered The Corrections “the last major American work of pre-9/11 literature—a historical document that depicts ordinary American life in a way that had been rendered obsolete.” But the novel is more than that: The Corrections is among the last genuine claimants to the status of the Great American Novel, the honorific for the chimerical and quixotic multi-generational, narratively complex, largely social realist work that explains the nation in all of its complexities to itself. 

While the September 11 novel by the “other” literary Jonathan (Safran Foer), Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close (2003), tends toward the maudlin and Don DeLillo’s Falling Man (2007) toward the overly cerebral, The Corrections felt exact precisely because it was not actually about September 11. Michiko Kakutani’s review in the New York Times came out on September 4 and was largely positive (comparing Franzen to Thomas Mann), though it leavened praise with the charge of its being “self-indulgent and long-winded.” (Franzen, never one to measure his words, later called the critic the “stupidest person in New York City.”) 

The Corrections is a novel about many things—the passing of generations and the internal incomprehensibility of families, the Internet and gentrification, the economics of finance and technology, struggling writers and celebrity chefs, and the place of the United States in the world. Which is to say that it is a novel of 2026 as well as of 2001. 

The Lamberts of St. Jude, Missouri, a town not all that different from Franzen’s native Webster Groves outside St. Louis, are presented as staid stalwarts of Midwestern, Protestant stoicism. Depending on your own personal disposition, the Lamberts may appear likable or not. (Their creator possesses something of the same conditional likability.) An epic in miniature, The Corrections toggles between elderly parents Alfred and Enid, the first a retired railroad engineer filled with misplaced corporate loyalty and suffering from Parkinson’s and dementia, while the latter is simply long-suffering. Enid wants nothing more than to bring her three children home for a final Christmas, which provides much of the novel’s narrative thrust. These prodigal sons and daughters include her oldest son Gary (a profoundly depressed Philadelphia bank executive whose family life is crumbling); the middle child Chip (a failed New York novelist and academic who absconds to Lithuania to take part in an online scam); and Denise (a promising chef living in the same city as her oldest brother who gets entangled in a psychologically knotty romance with a married couple).

Franzen’s depiction of each of the Lambert children seems to anticipate more recent trends: Gary’s marital relationship and emotional stability are as precarious as a 2008 stock report; Chip draws more meaning from scamming Lithuanian retirees than from his own writing, calling to mind the late-2010s golden era of bot farms; and Denise’s dreams of being a celebrity chef run aground in her adventure in polyamory, now a minor phenomenon. 

Throughout Franzen’s pages sounds a quiet, steady drone, a faint noise that even the author might not have been able to hear as clearly as he would in the coming decades—one that represents the approach not only of September 11 but also of the financial collapse as well as the Internet’s psychic ubiquity. As Franzen writes, unwittingly elegiacally, “elective ignorance was a great survival skill, perhaps the greatest.” To read The Corrections after twenty-five years is to see America through a mirror darkly, as a country more prosperous and carefree, yet still overshadowed by a spiritual malignancy not yet tangible.

Although it is by far his most acclaimed novel, The Corrections was a departure from the showy postmodernism of his first two books, particularly his 1988 debut, The Twenty-Seventh City. The Corrections is often thought of as a “systems novel,” what critic Tom LeClair understood as a kind of maximalist endeavor intending to understand interconnected networks in all of their complexity, in this case, making the Lamberts—the materialistic but spiritually dead Gary, Chip the grifting gig worker, and Denise the aspiring gentrifier—representative of the social world of post–Cold War American neoliberalism. Franzen himself chafed at the characterization. In a 2002 essay for The New Yorker, aptly titled “Mr. Difficult,” Franzen claimed he “didn’t particularly like the writers in my modern canon”—that is, Thomas Pynchon and William Gaddis, Donald Barthelme and Robert Coover, preferring Dickens and Dostoevsky. A temperamental and aesthetic conservative, if not a political one, Franzen nonetheless admitted to craving the “academic and hipster respect of the kind that Pynchon and Gaddis” received, or, it could be said, that which his friend David Foster Wallace benefited from, even while he “unhiply enjoyed reading” Saul Bellow. Indeed, there is more in The Corrections of Updike’s Rabbit books than there is of Gaddis’s The Recognitions. 

Like The Strokes’ acclaimed debut album Is This It released five weeks before the 9/11 attacks, The Corrections benefited in a perverse way from the violence of that day in its elevation to oracular status. Yet Franzen’s narrative command, his gift for dialogue, and his ability to explore major social, political, economic, and cultural themes without recourse to mere didacticism (a skill many authors in the subsequent generation abandoned) make the accolades received by the novel on its release all the more understandable. Ranging as it does from suburban Missouri to Manhattan to Vilnius and a North Atlantic cruise ship, The Corrections displays the maximalism and gravitas that allows it to be considered a Great American Novel.

If the novel, with its WASPiness and its unabashed middle-Americanism, is among the last of this type of novel to be taken seriously as such by critics, the critical audience for such a work has largely fallen away since its publication, eroded by a growing cultural bellicosity and authoritarianism, as well as the collapse of an intellectual monoculture, which christened particular novels as deserving of being both “Great” and “American,” as if those adjectives still belonged together. Tellingly, when The Guardian made its 2026 list of the best novels of all time, The Corrections didn’t make the cut, perhaps because Europeans have grown justifiably tired of American literary navel-gazing. 

Franzen himself is “Mr. Difficult,” if not a difficult writer (though he’s also clearly a humane and empathetic one). Despite being profanely funnier than he often has any right to be (remember that Alfred Lambert, with shades of the constipated Martin Luther, hallucinates a wise-cracking anthropomorphic turd), there often remains a grumpy, Midwestern, Protestant work ethic seriousness about Franzen, the Swarthmore creative writing instructor who supposedly wrote “Truth” and “Beauty” on the blackboard the first day of class and told his students that those were the only goals of serious fiction—the author who in a 2002 interview with The Guardian could say, “Today’s Baudelaires are hip-hop artists” as if he were a high school’s cringiest English teacher, the sort of curmudgeon who alienates fellow birders by taking on the National Audubon Society for focusing more on climate change than threatened bird habitats. 

Then there was the Oprah incident. Shortly after The Corrections was published, Oprah anointed it as a selection for her book club, prompting Franzen to worry that the coveted gold cover sticker would relegate it to books that have a “schmaltzy, one-dimensional kind of benefit-and-uplift-sensibility.” Ms. Winfrey was not amused, and the invitation to appear on the show was rescinded, although she would invite him to appear when his next novel, Freedom, came out in 2010. Yet part of the reason Franzen seems to have earned the title of American literature’s most punchable face is not just because he is sometimes wrong but because he is so frequently right. At the turn of the century Oprah’s Book Club was understandably perceived as a literary beacon in an increasingly coarse culture, but Franzen was not the kind of person who would lend himself and his reputation to enhancing the likes of Dr. Phil, Dr. Oz, and John of God. And Franzen’s warnings about technology now sound less like harangues than prophecies in the era of AI, water-hungry data centers, Flock cameras, and deepfakes. “The aim of the Internet and its associated technologies was to ‘liberate’ humanity from the tasks—making things, learnings things, remembering things—that had previously given meaning to life,” Franzen wrote in his 2015 novel Purity. At the time that sounded alarmist; a decade later it sounds commonsensical. 

Appropriately enough, one reason the Great American Novel cannot be written anymore, by Franzen or anyone else, is the death of what we call “middlebrow culture.” Part of Franzen’s anxiety over the Oprah Book Club selection was his fear of being thought of as middlebrow. Yet, in 2001, that is precisely what The Corrections was. And there should be no shame attached to that fact. Franzen’s readers are the same ones who were drawn to Updikes and Bellow rather than the arch postmodernists. His fiction was meant to be accessible and to speak to a community of readers. “A novel is a compact between the writer and the reader,” Franzen wrote in a 2011 piece in The New Yorker, whereby “Fiction is the most fundamental human art.” That essay, “Mr. Difficult,” details in a loving way his own wrestling with the experimental work of Gaddis, but the broader point that Franzen makes is about the democratic utility of literature, a humanistic argument about why we read books—back when we read them. During the mid-century, the middlebrow was the domain of Masterpiece Theatre and Leonard Bernstein, the “Book of the Month Club,” and public television. Now that there is only lowbrow and ever-shrinking highbrow, we can’t even recognize the venerable middlebrow when it appears. (Nowhere is this more obvious than the category errors plaguing Christopher Nolan’s 2026 film The Odyssey.) In his essay, Franzen wrote that a “difficult novel just sits there on your shelf unread,” and he wasn’t wrong. Now, when according to The Atlantic only 38 percent of Americans read a book in the last year, it appears that easy novels sit unread on shelves as much as difficult ones. 

The Corrections is not the last Great American Novel because great American novels have ceased to be written. Plenty have been published, many as good as or better than The Corrections, including Philip Roth’s speculative but personal The Plot Against America, Marilynne Robinson’s Gilead with its quiet spiritualism, Michael Chabon’s spectacular The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay, George Saunders’s mystical Lincoln in the Bardo, and the unforgettable The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao by Junot Díaz. Franzen’s is the last of a type because the cultural circumstances in which such a thing could even be understood have disappeared in an increasingly disparate and atomized society. Now, when middlebrow has completely collapsed and Oprah’s Book Club has been replaced by BookTok—on which novels are just as likely to be used as props as to be read—then how fortunate that The Corrections, in its own inadvertent way, acted as a kind of auto-obituary for the very form, an astute and moving elegy on all that was being lost. 

Since The Corrections was published, Americans witnessed not only September 11 but all that has come after: Afghanistan and Iraq, radio bans and freedom fries, Covid and artificial intelligence, the alt-right and January 6, 2021, and, of course, Trump himself. Now, in 2026, after Facebook and Instagram, Twitter, and TikTok, who could possibly imagine any single book being lauded by the press, insomuch as the press still exists, as the “Great American Novel,” as a summing up of the United States in all of its contradictions and complexities while orienting the reader toward the nation’s noblest ideals? In 2010, Franzen appeared on the cover of Time, with his thick black glasses and floppy, graying hair appearing as the very serious little boy that he so often presents in the media, the words “Great American Novelist” affixed in glowing white print in the corner. The last time a fiction author appeared on the cover of the country’s most venerable middlebrow publication was Stephen King in 2000. No novelist since Franzen has made the cut.
